theme: The gentle answer; God weighs the heart; friendship
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 15:1-17:28. As you read, look for what these chapters teach about words, the heart, and the sovereignty of God over human plans.
settingTheScene: These chapters continue the Solomonic collection, and now more sayings speak directly about the LORD. They deal with the gentle answer, the way God sees the heart, plans and God’s purposes, pride, and friendship. Chapter 16 in particular grapples with how human planning and divine control fit together.
observation: “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (15:1).
“The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (15:3).
“Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed” (15:22).
“All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit” (16:2).
“Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established” (16:3).
“The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (16:9).
“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (16:18).
“A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (17:17).
interpretation:
The famous opening line of chapter 15 gives a practical truth: “A soft answer turns away wrath.” A gentle word can defuse a conflict. The next lines contrast the wise tongue with the foolish mouth, and show that the way we speak reflects the state of our hearts. The whole section turns often to the tongue: “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit.”

Verse 3 says that “the eyes of the LORD are in every place.” It can be a comfort or a warning. For the one who hides, it is a warning. For the one who walks in integrity, it is a comfort. God sees. We are not unobserved, and we are not forgotten.

Chapter 16 sets a key principle of Christian life: our planning and God’s sovereignty. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.” We should make plans. The Bible does not say planning is wrong. But we hold them with open hands. God has the final say. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.” Even what looks like chance is under his rule. This does not make us passive. It makes us humble and trusting. “Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established.”

Verse 2 is a warning about self-assessment: “All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.” We tend to judge ourselves by our intentions and others by their actions. God weighs the heart. And the famous verse 18 warns about pride, “before a fall.” The humble in spirit, by contrast, are described as better off than the proud.

Chapter 17 includes a series of sayings about friendship and family: “A friend loves at all times.” “A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.” And it also warns about quarreling. “The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out.”
connection: Jesus, “when he was reviled, did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), and taught that blessed are the meek (Matthew 5:5). Paul wrote, “Let your speech always be gracious” (Colossians 4:6). James 4:13-15 echoes Proverbs 16:9: “You ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live.” Jesus, the friend of sinners (Luke 7:34), is “a friend who sticks closer than a brother.” Romans 8:28 holds God’s sovereignty and our good together.
application:
In your next tense conversation, try a soft answer.

Hold one of your plans loosely today. Commit it to the LORD, and notice what changes.

Consider where you judge yourself by your intentions, and ask God to weigh your heart.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you gentle answers.
Ask him to establish your steps and keep you from pride.
Thank him that he weighs the spirit with perfect knowledge.
